summary:
Maryland's gender-identity law is protective. The Fairness for All Marylanders Act of 2014, effective 1 October 2014, prohibits discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations statewide; before that date protection existed only in Baltimore City, Baltimore County, Howard County, Hyattsville and Montgomery County. Discrimination based on sexual orientation has been prohibited statewide since the Antidiscrimination Act of 2001 took effect on 21 November 2001.

The hate-crime statute adds penalties for crimes motivated by actual or perceived gender identity, listed as a separate category by an amendment effective 1 October 2021. HB231, effective the same date, abolished the common-law gay and trans panic defence.

A 2024 law declaring Maryland a sanctuary state for the protection and defence of transgender individuals passed the Senate 33-13 and the House 97-38 and was signed by Governor Wes Moore, effective 1 October 2024. It followed a June 2023 executive order protecting unimpeded access to gender-affirming healthcare and an insurance law effective 1 January 2024 described in state-by-state rights research as the most transgender healthcare friendly in the United States.

Maryland stands under the United States federal framework. Passport and visa sex markers, federal facility rules, immigration detention and federal custody are governed nationally, not by the state.

State-level identity documents are accessible but not complete. Since 1 October 2015 a birth-certificate gender marker can be changed without surgery or sterilisation on certification from a licensed healthcare provider confirming gender identity; the X marker remained unavailable on Maryland birth certificates as of 2023. Motor Vehicle Administration IDs and voter registration have allowed X since 1 October 2019 without legal or medical documentation, and the University of Maryland will add X in 2026. HB39, effective 1 October 2021, repealed the 1971 requirement to publish a name in a newspaper before a legal change on a birth certificate.

Facilities and student access run in favour of transgender people. In March 2018 a federal court ruled that transgender students may use restrooms and locker rooms consistent with gender identity, striking down a Talbot County policy; Montgomery County adopted gender-neutral bathroom requirements by a 9-0 vote in July 2022 and Baltimore does so by ordinance. A February 2022 county report records that transgender athletes may participate according to gender identity without proof, documentation, or medical or legal transition, after bills in 2022 and 2023 that would have restricted teams by biological sex failed.

Violence against transgender people in Maryland is documented. On 11 September 2026 Sophie Lee, a 27-year-old Black trans woman, was found shot in Baltimore's Charles Village and died; she was the second Black trans woman shot to death in Baltimore within ten weeks.

Protection machinery includes Montgomery County's unanimous October 2020 LGBTIQ+ bill of rights ordinance, a 15-member Commission on LGBTIQ+ Affairs created by HB130 effective October 2021 and expanded to 21 members in April 2023, and HB1380, effective 1 October 2022, which automatically restores honorable discharges retrospectively to LGBT individuals who lived in Maryland at the time.

Marriage between people of the same sex has been legal in Maryland since 1 January 2013 under the Civil Marriage Protection Act, approved 72-67 in the House on 17 February 2012 and 25-22 in the Senate on 23 February 2012, signed 1 March 2012 and approved by 52.4% of voters on 6 November 2012, after a 1973 ban; domestic partnerships have existed since 2008 and out-of-state marriages have been recognised since 2010. A trans visitor whose relationship Maryland law reads as same-sex under birth-sex status can marry here.
tangentialFactors:
A July 2026 analysis plotting recorded anti-trans incidents against each state's law score places Maryland in its 'Safest States' band with a law score of 23.5 and 11.1 recorded incidents, while Louisiana records both the worst laws (24.7) and 11.6 recorded incidents. The analysis's finding is that protective law floors do not by themselves predict recorded incident counts. The figures are state-level totals; the material reviewed supplies no per-capita denominator, so rankings of this kind track population size as well as risk and should not be read as a comparison of individual danger.

The state's sexual-practices statute has its own enforcement history. Court rulings in Schochet v. State in 1990 and Williams v. Glendening in October 1998 invalidated the prohibition on private consensual oral sex, and a 1999 settlement covered anal sex. Legislative repeal of the anal-sex provision took effect 1 October 2020 and repeal of the oral-sex ban passed in 2023 and took effect 1 October 2023 without Governor Wes Moore's signature. In July 2021 several men were arrested for conduct that was not criminalised when engaged in heterosexually, under the Unnatural or Perverted Sexual Practices Act, which remained on the books because the 2020 Senate amendment left the oral-sex ban intact after a 2022 repeal attempt died in committee.
localsOnly:
Residents have broad public coverage for gender-affirming treatment. Medicaid explicitly covers sexual reassignment surgery for eligible residents over 18 under a bill passed in March 2023, signed in April 2023, and effective 1 January 2024. The Trans Health Equity Act, sponsored by Del. Anne Kaiser, D-Montgomery, passed the House of Delegates as of 20 May 2024 to extend Medicaid coverage of gender-affirming treatment and awaited action in the Maryland Senate.

Conversion therapy by licensed practitioners on minors has been prohibited since 1 October 2018, after passage in April 2018 and signature in May 2018; a federal constitutional challenge was dismissed in September 2019.
outOfScopeNotes:
No documented Maryland rule on housing transgender prisoners, no dedicated unit and no named case appears in the sources reviewed, so how the state places transgender people in custody is unresolved here.

The sources give no general homicide rate for Baltimore or for Maryland, so whether the two killings in ten weeks exceed the background risk in the city is not established; the ten-week count is a raw figure without a denominator.

The Senate outcome of the Trans Health Equity Act is not recorded in the sources, and whether the 2024 sanctuary law extends its protections to non-resident visitors is not sourced.
